Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 56, verse 1–12:

(p-130) Surat al-Waqi'ah (The Inevitable Event)

Regarding it there are two opinions.

One of them: it is Meccan. This was said by most scholars, among them Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, 'Ata', 'Ikrimah, Qatadah, Jabir and Muqatil. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that it contains one Medinan verse, which is His saying: ﴿And you make your provision that you deny?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 82]

The second: it is Medinan. This was narrated by 'Atiyyah from Ibn 'Abbas.

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿When the Inevitable Event befalls﴾. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: When the disbelievers said, "When is this promise? When is this victory?!" the saying ﴿When the Inevitable Event befalls﴾ was revealed. So the meaning is: when the Inevitable Event occurs. The commentators said: al-Waqi'ah is the Resurrection, and everything that is awaited and comes is said, when it has come about, to have "befallen" (waqa'a). What is meant here is the blowing into the Trumpet for the rising of the Hour.

(p-131) ﴿There is no denying its befalling﴾, i.e., its manifestation and coming. "Kadhibah" means a lie, as in His saying: ﴿You will not hear therein any idle talk﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 11], i.e., vain talk. al-Zajjaj said: "Kadhibah" is a verbal noun (masdar), as in your saying: "Allah granted him 'afiyah (well-being)" and "he lied kadhibah", so these are nouns in the place of the verbal noun. There are two opinions regarding the meaning of the statement.

One of them: there is no return from it and no turning back; this was said by Qatadah. The second: the report of its occurrence is not a lie; this was related by al-Mawardi.

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Abasing (khafidah)﴾, i.e., it abases ﴿and exalting (rafi'ah)﴾. Abu Razin, Abu 'Abd al-Rahman, Abu al-'Aliyah, al-Hasan, Ibn Abi 'Ablah, Abu Haywah, and al-Yazidi in his choice read "khafidatan rafi'atan" in the accusative in both. There are two opinions regarding the meaning of the statement.

One of them: it lowers and so makes the near hear, and raises and so makes the far hear; this was narrated by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas. This indicates that what is meant by the Inevitable Event is the Cry of the Resurrection.

The second: it lowers some people and raises others; this was narrated by 'Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas. The commentators said: it lowers groups to the lowest of the low in the Fire, and raises groups to 'Illiyyin in the Garden.

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿When the earth is shaken with a violent shaking (rajjan)﴾, i.e., it is moved with a severe movement and convulsed. That is because it quakes until whatever buildings are on it collapse and whatever mountains are on it crumble. Regarding its quaking there are two opinions.

One of them: it is to cause the living upon it to die. The second: it is to bring out those in its belly of the dead.

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿And the mountains will be crumbled to dust (bassan)﴾. Regarding it there are two opinions.

(p-132) One of them: they will be pulverized into powder; this was narrated by Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas, and Mujahid said likewise. Ibn Qutaybah said: they will be pulverized until they become like flour and sawiq (roasted meal) that has been kneaded.

The second: they will be mixed up; this was said by Qatadah. al-Zajjaj said: they will be mixed and kneaded. The poet said:

Do not bake bread of kneaded (khabzan wa bussan bassan) ...

Regarding "al-Habaa" there are opinions which we have mentioned at [al-Furqan: 23]. Ibn Qutaybah mentioned that "al-habaa al-munbaththu" is what rises from the hooves of horses, and it is from "al-hab'ah," and al-hab'ah is dust. The meaning is: they will be scattered dust.

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿And you will be three kinds (azwaja)﴾, i.e., categories, "three".

"Then the companions of the right (ashab al-maymanah)" — regarding them there are eight opinions.

One of them: they are those who were on the right of Adam when his offspring were brought forth from his loins; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: they are those who will be given their records in their right hands; this was said by al-Dahhak and al-Qurazi.

The third: they are those who were blessed (mayamin) upon themselves, i.e., blessed; this was said by al-Hasan and al-Rabi'.

The fourth: they are those who were taken from Adam's right side; this was said by Zayd ibn Aslam.

The fifth: they are those whose station is on the right; this was said by Maymun ibn Mihran.

The sixth: they are the people of Paradise; this was said by al-Suddi.

The seventh: they are the companions of the lofty station; this was said by al-Zajjaj.

(p-133) The eighth: they are those who will be taken to the Garden by the right side; this was mentioned by 'Ali ibn Ahmad al-Nisaburi.

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿What are the companions of the right?﴾ al-Farra' said: He marvels at them to His Prophet (ﷺ); the meaning is: what are they?! al-Zajjaj said: this expression in Arabic is in the manner of amazement, and when it comes from God, the Mighty and Majestic, in addressing His servants, it magnifies the matter in their sight, like ﴿What is the Inevitable Reality?﴾ [al-Haqqah: 2] and ﴿What is the Striking Calamity?﴾ [al-Qari'ah: 2]. Ibn Qutaybah said: similar to it is one saying: "Zayd, what Zayd is!" i.e., what a man he is! ﴿And the companions of the left, what are the companions of the left?﴾ [i.e., the companions of] the left. The Arabs call the left hand "al-Shu'ma" and the left side "al-Ash'am," and from this come the words "al-yumn" (blessing) and "al-shu'm" (ill omen): yumn is as if it came from the right, and shu'm came from the left. From this "Yemen" and "Sham" were named, because they lie to the right and left of the Ka'bah. The commentators said: the companions of the right are those who will be taken to the right, and who will be given their records in their right hands; the interpretation of the companions of the left is the opposite of the interpretation of the companions of the right, equally; the meaning is: what people are they?! What torment has been prepared for them?!

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿And the foremost, the foremost﴾. Regarding them there are five opinions.

One of them: they are the foremost to faith from every nation; this was said by al-Hasan and Qatadah. The second: they are those who prayed towards both qiblahs; this was said by Ibn Sirin. The third: they are the people of the Qur'an; this was said by Ka'b. The fourth: they are the Prophets; this was said by Muhammad ibn Ka'b. The fifth: they are the foremost to the mosques and to going out in the way of Allah; this was said by 'Uthman ibn Abi Sawdah.

Regarding the repetition of their mention there are two opinions.

(p-134) One of them: that is for emphasis. The second: the meaning is that the foremost to the obedience of Allah are the foremost to the mercy of Allah; both were mentioned by al-Zajjaj.

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Those are the ones brought near (al-muqarraboon)﴾. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: meaning near to Allah, in the shade of His Throne and in His neighborhood.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 56, verse 1–12:

(p-130) Surat al-Waqi'ah (The Inevitable Event)

Regarding it there are two opinions.

One of them: it is Meccan. This was said by most scholars, among them Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, 'Ata', 'Ikrimah, Qatadah, Jabir and Muqatil. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that it contains one Medinan verse, which is His saying: ﴿And you make your provision that you deny?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 82]

The second: it is Medinan. This was narrated by 'Atiyyah from Ibn 'Abbas.

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿When the Inevitable Event befalls﴾. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: When the disbelievers said, "When is this promise? When is this victory?!" the saying ﴿When the Inevitable Event befalls﴾ was revealed. So the meaning is: when the Inevitable Event occurs. The commentators said: al-Waqi'ah is the Resurrection, and everything that is awaited and comes is said, when it has come about, to have "befallen" (waqa'a). What is meant here is the blowing into the Trumpet for the rising of the Hour.

(p-131) ﴿There is no denying its befalling﴾, i.e., its manifestation and coming. "Kadhibah" means a lie, as in His saying: ﴿You will not hear therein any idle talk﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 11], i.e., vain talk. al-Zajjaj said: "Kadhibah" is a verbal noun (masdar), as in your saying: "Allah granted him 'afiyah (well-being)" and "he lied kadhibah", so these are nouns in the place of the verbal noun. There are two opinions regarding the meaning of the statement.

One of them: there is no return from it and no turning back; this was said by Qatadah. The second: the report of its occurrence is not a lie; this was related by al-Mawardi.

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Abasing (khafidah)﴾, i.e., it abases ﴿and exalting (rafi'ah)﴾. Abu Razin, Abu 'Abd al-Rahman, Abu al-'Aliyah, al-Hasan, Ibn Abi 'Ablah, Abu Haywah, and al-Yazidi in his choice read "khafidatan rafi'atan" in the accusative in both. There are two opinions regarding the meaning of the statement.

One of them: it lowers and so makes the near hear, and raises and so makes the far hear; this was narrated by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas. This indicates that what is meant by the Inevitable Event is the Cry of the Resurrection.

The second: it lowers some people and raises others; this was narrated by 'Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas. The commentators said: it lowers groups to the lowest of the low in the Fire, and raises groups to 'Illiyyin in the Garden.

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿When the earth is shaken with a violent shaking (rajjan)﴾, i.e., it is moved with a severe movement and convulsed. That is because it quakes until whatever buildings are on it collapse and whatever mountains are on it crumble. Regarding its quaking there are two opinions.

One of them: it is to cause the living upon it to die. The second: it is to bring out those in its belly of the dead.

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿And the mountains will be crumbled to dust (bassan)﴾. Regarding it there are two opinions.

(p-132) One of them: they will be pulverized into powder; this was narrated by Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas, and Mujahid said likewise. Ibn Qutaybah said: they will be pulverized until they become like flour and sawiq (roasted meal) that has been kneaded.

The second: they will be mixed up; this was said by Qatadah. al-Zajjaj said: they will be mixed and kneaded. The poet said:

Do not bake bread of kneaded (khabzan wa bussan bassan) ...

Regarding "al-Habaa" there are opinions which we have mentioned at [al-Furqan: 23]. Ibn Qutaybah mentioned that "al-habaa al-munbaththu" is what rises from the hooves of horses, and it is from "al-hab'ah," and al-hab'ah is dust. The meaning is: they will be scattered dust.

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿And you will be three kinds (azwaja)﴾, i.e., categories, "three".

"Then the companions of the right (ashab al-maymanah)" — regarding them there are eight opinions.

One of them: they are those who were on the right of Adam when his offspring were brought forth from his loins; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: they are those who will be given their records in their right hands; this was said by al-Dahhak and al-Qurazi.

The third: they are those who were blessed (mayamin) upon themselves, i.e., blessed; this was said by al-Hasan and al-Rabi'.

The fourth: they are those who were taken from Adam's right side; this was said by Zayd ibn Aslam.

The fifth: they are those whose station is on the right; this was said by Maymun ibn Mihran.

The sixth: they are the people of Paradise; this was said by al-Suddi.

The seventh: they are the companions of the lofty station; this was said by al-Zajjaj.

(p-133) The eighth: they are those who will be taken to the Garden by the right side; this was mentioned by 'Ali ibn Ahmad al-Nisaburi.

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿What are the companions of the right?﴾ al-Farra' said: He marvels at them to His Prophet (ﷺ); the meaning is: what are they?! al-Zajjaj said: this expression in Arabic is in the manner of amazement, and when it comes from God, the Mighty and Majestic, in addressing His servants, it magnifies the matter in their sight, like ﴿What is the Inevitable Reality?﴾ [al-Haqqah: 2] and ﴿What is the Striking Calamity?﴾ [al-Qari'ah: 2]. Ibn Qutaybah said: similar to it is one saying: "Zayd, what Zayd is!" i.e., what a man he is! ﴿And the companions of the left, what are the companions of the left?﴾ [i.e., the companions of] the left. The Arabs call the left hand "al-Shu'ma" and the left side "al-Ash'am," and from this come the words "al-yumn" (blessing) and "al-shu'm" (ill omen): yumn is as if it came from the right, and shu'm came from the left. From this "Yemen" and "Sham" were named, because they lie to the right and left of the Ka'bah. The commentators said: the companions of the right are those who will be taken to the right, and who will be given their records in their right hands; the interpretation of the companions of the left is the opposite of the interpretation of the companions of the right, equally; the meaning is: what people are they?! What torment has been prepared for them?!

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿And the foremost, the foremost﴾. Regarding them there are five opinions.

One of them: they are the foremost to faith from every nation; this was said by al-Hasan and Qatadah. The second: they are those who prayed towards both qiblahs; this was said by Ibn Sirin. The third: they are the people of the Qur'an; this was said by Ka'b. The fourth: they are the Prophets; this was said by Muhammad ibn Ka'b. The fifth: they are the foremost to the mosques and to going out in the way of Allah; this was said by 'Uthman ibn Abi Sawdah.

Regarding the repetition of their mention there are two opinions.

(p-134) One of them: that is for emphasis. The second: the meaning is that the foremost to the obedience of Allah are the foremost to the mercy of Allah; both were mentioned by al-Zajjaj.

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Those are the ones brought near (al-muqarraboon)﴾. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: meaning near to Allah, in the shade of His Throne and in His neighborhood.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 56, verse 13–26:

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿A multitude of the former peoples﴾. Thullah (a multitude) means a group whose number is not restricted.

Regarding "the former ones" and "the latter ones" here, there are three opinions.

The first: the "former ones" are those who lived from the time of Adam to the time of our Prophet ﷺ, and the "latter ones" are this Ummah.

The second: the "former ones" are the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and the "latter ones" are the Successors (al-Tabi'un).

The third: the "former and latter ones" are from among the Companions of our Prophet Muhammad ﷺ.

According to the first opinion, the meaning is: the foremost ones (al-sabiqun) are a multitude from the earlier nations, who preceded others in affirming their prophets, and a few from the Ummah of Muhammad ﷺ, because those who witnessed all the prophets and believed in them are more numerous than those who witnessed our Prophet and believed in him.

(p-135) According to the second: the foremost ones are a group of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, namely the earliest of the Emigrants (Muhajirun) and the Helpers (Ansar), and a few of the Successors, who followed them with excellence.

According to the third: the foremost ones are the earliest of the Emigrants and the Helpers, and a few of those who came after them, because the later ones are unable to reach the earliest ones, so only a few of them come close to them in precedence.

As for "mawdunah" (woven), Ibn Qutaybah said: it means interwoven, as if some of it is inserted into other parts, or some of it is arranged upon other parts. From this comes the term for a coat of mail: mawdunah. From this also comes the term wadin (girth) of the she-camel, which is a band of straps where one part is inserted into another. Al-Farra' said: I heard some of the Arabs say: "The brick is mawdun, one part upon another," meaning mushraj (laid in layers).

Regarding the meaning of "mawdunah," the exegetes have two opinions.

The first: it means inlaid with gold, related by Mujahid from Ibn Abbas. Ikrimah said: interlaced with pearls and rubies. This is the meaning of what we mentioned from Ibn Qutaybah, and most scholars hold this view.

The second: arranged in rows, related by Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn Abbas.

What follows has already been explained [al-Kahf: 30], up to His saying: ﴿Youths made eternal﴾. Wildan (youths) means boys. Al-Hasan al-Basri said: these are children who had no good deeds for which they would be rewarded, nor evil deeds for which they would be punished, so they were placed in this position.

Regarding "mukhalladun" (made eternal), there are two opinions.

The first: it is from khuld (eternity), and the meaning is that they are created to remain, not changing, and they are of one age. Al-Farra' said: the Arabs say of a person who has grown old but whose hair has not turned gray, or whose teeth have not fallen out due to old age: "He is indeed mukhalladun." This is the view of the majority.

(p-136) The second: they are those adorned with earrings; it is also said: those adorned with bracelets. Al-Farra' and Ibn Qutaybah mentioned this, and they cited in support:

"And mukhalladat (ornamented) with silver, as if their hindquarters were the dunes' sandhills."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿With cups and ewers﴾. The kub (cup) is a vessel with no handle and no spout, and we have mentioned it in [al-Zukhruf: 71]. The abariq (ewers) are vessels that have handles and spouts. I read to our shaykh Abu Mansur al-Lughawi, who said: al-Ibriq is a Persian word that has been Arabized, and its translation from Persian is one of two things: either "the path of water," or "pouring water in ease." The Arabs have used it in ancient times. 'Adi ibn Zayd said:

"He called for the morning drink one day, and there came a singing-girl with an ibriq in her right hand."

For the rest of the verses, see [al-Saffat: 46].

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They will not be affected with headache thereby nor will they be intoxicated﴾. Regarding this, there are two opinions.

The first: no headache will afflict them, as afflicts the drinkers of the wine of this world. "Thereby" refers to the cup mentioned, and what is meant is the wine. This is the view of the majority.

The second: they will not be scattered away from it, from your saying: "I split it and it split," related by Ibn Qutaybah. As for "yunzifun" (intoxicated), it is explained in [al-Saffat: 47].

(p-137) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿From what they choose﴾, i.e., what they select. You say: "I chose the thing" when you take its best part.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the flesh of fowl﴾. Ibn Abbas said: the bird comes to mind, and it appears before him, as he desires. Mughith ibn Sumayy said: birds like camels rest upon the branches of the tree of Tuba; when a man desires a bird, he calls it, and it comes and lands upon his table, and he eats from one side of it roasted meat and from the other side grilled meat, then it returns as a bird and flies away.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And fair-eyed houris﴾. Ibn Kathir, 'Asim, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, and Ibn 'Amir recited "wa-hurun 'in" with nominative (raf') in both. Abu Ja'far, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and al-Mufaddal from 'Asim recited with genitive (khafd) in both. Ubayy ibn Ka'b, 'A'ishah, Abu al-'Aliyah, and 'Asim al-Jahdari recited "wa-huran 'inan" with accusative (nasb) in both. Al-Zajjaj said: Those who recited the nominative disliked the genitive, because it is coordinated with His saying "yatufu 'alayhim" (they will be served by), and they said: the houris are not among the things that are served around. But it is in the genitive according to a different interpretation from what these people held: the meaning is that youths made eternal serve them with cups from which they take pleasure, and likewise they take pleasure in the flesh of fowl, and likewise they take pleasure in fair-eyed houris. The nominative is better, and the meaning is: and for them are fair-eyed houris. Whoever recited "wa-huran 'inan" in the accusative understood it according to the sense, because the meaning is: they are given these things and they are given fair-eyed houris; however, it contradicts the written codex (mushaf), so it is disliked. The meaning of "like pearls well-guarded" is that their clarity and luster are like the clarity and luster of pearls. "Maknun" (well-guarded) is that which time and the variation of conditions of use have not altered; thus they are like pearls when they come out of their shell.

(p-138) "Jaza'an" (as a reward) is in the accusative as an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu). The meaning: this is done for them as a reward for their deeds. It may also be accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), because the meaning of "yatufu 'alayhim wildanun mukhalladun" is: they are recompensed as a reward for their deeds; and most grammarians hold this view.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They will not hear therein any vain talk﴾. We have already explained the meaning of laghw (vain talk) and salam (peace) in Surat Maryam [19:62], the meaning of ta'thim (sinful speech) in [al-Tur: 23], and the meaning of ﴿What are the companions of the right hand?﴾ at the beginning of this surah [al-Waqi'ah: 9].

If it is said: ta'thim is not heard, so how did He mention it with what is heard?

The answer: the Arabs make the end of a speech follow its beginning, even if what suits one of them does not suit the other. They say: "I ate bread and milk," though milk is not eaten; this is acceptable only because it was with what is eaten. Al-Farra' said: one of the Arabs recited to me:

"When the courtesans come forth one day, and they darken their eyebrows and eyes."

He said: The eye is not darkened with kohl; rather it is applied with kohl, but he attributed it to the eyebrow because the meaning is understood. Another recited to me:

"I met your husband in battle, girded with a sword and a spear."

Another recited to me:

"I fed her straw and cold water."

Water is not fed; it is drunk, but he made it follow the straw. Al-Farra' said: this is (p-139) the reading of whoever recited "wa-hurin 'in" in the genitive, by making the end of the speech follow its beginning, and this is the way of Arabic.

He said: The eye is not darkened with kohl; rather it is applied with kohl, but he attributed it to the eyebrow because the meaning is understood. Another recited to me:

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿A multitude of the former peoples﴾. Thullah (a multitude) means a group whose number is not restricted.

Regarding "the former ones" and "the latter ones" here, there are three opinions.

The first: the "former ones" are those who lived from the time of Adam to the time of our Prophet ﷺ, and the "latter ones" are this Ummah.

The second: the "former ones" are the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and the "latter ones" are the Successors (al-Tabi'un).

The third: the "former and latter ones" are from among the Companions of our Prophet Muhammad ﷺ.

According to the first opinion, the meaning is: the foremost ones (al-sabiqun) are a multitude from the earlier nations, who preceded others in affirming their prophets, and a few from the Ummah of Muhammad ﷺ, because those who witnessed all the prophets and believed in them are more numerous than those who witnessed our Prophet and believed in him.

(p-135) According to the second: the foremost ones are a group of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, namely the earliest of the Emigrants (Muhajirun) and the Helpers (Ansar), and a few of the Successors, who followed them with excellence.

According to the third: the foremost ones are the earliest of the Emigrants and the Helpers, and a few of those who came after them, because the later ones are unable to reach the earliest ones, so only a few of them come close to them in precedence.

From this comes the term for a coat of mail: mawdunah. From this also comes the term wadin (girth) of the she-camel, which is a band of straps where one part is inserted into another. Al-Farra' said: I heard some of the Arabs say: "The brick is mawdun, one part upon another," meaning mushraj (laid in layers).

Regarding the meaning of "mawdunah," the exegetes have two opinions.

The first: it means inlaid with gold, related by Mujahid from Ibn Abbas. Ikrimah said: interlaced with pearls and rubies. This is the meaning of what we mentioned from Ibn Qutaybah, and most scholars hold this view.

The second: arranged in rows, related by Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn Abbas.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 56, verse 27–40:

We have already explained the meaning of His saying ﴿and the companions of the right hand﴾ in His saying ﴿the companions of the right hand (al-maymanah)﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 9]. It has been related from ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "The companions of the right hand are the children of the believers."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Among lote trees with thorns removed﴾. The occasion of its revelation: the Muslims looked at Wajj, which is a valley in al-Ta'if, fertile, and its lote trees (sidr) impressed them, so they said: "Would that we had the like of this!" Then this verse was revealed. This was related by Abu al-ʿAliyah and al-Dahhak.

Regarding al-makhdud (with thorns removed) there are three opinions.

The first: it is the one that has no thorns. This was narrated by Abu Talhah from Ibn ʿAbbas, and ʿIkrimah and Qusamah ibn Zuhayr also said so. Ibn Qutaybah said: "It is as if its thorns were cut off (khudida), i.e., uprooted." From this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ about Madinah: "Its thorns shall not be cut off."

The second: it is the one laden with fruit. This was narrated by al-ʿAwfi from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Mujahid and al-Dahhak also said so.

The third: it is the one laden with fruit that has no thorns. This was mentioned by Qatadah.

Regarding al-talh (acacia) there are two opinions.

One: it is the banana tree (al-mawz). This was said by ʿAli, Ibn ʿAbbas, Abu Hurayrah, Abu Saʿid al-Khudri, [al-Hasan], ʿAta', ʿIkrimah, Mujahid and Qatadah.

The second: it is large trees with big thorns. Abu ʿUbaydah said: "This is the talh among the Arabs." The camel driver (al-Hadi) said:

*Her guide gave her good news and said: "Tomorrow you will see the acacia and the mountains."*

If it is asked: what is the benefit of the talh?

The answer: it has blossoms and a pleasant fragrance, so He promised them what they know and incline towards, even though there is no equality between it and what is in this world. Mujahid said: "They used to admire Wajj, its shade, its acacias and its lote trees." As for al-mandud (layered, arranged), Ibn Qutaybah said: "It is the one that is arranged with fruit or leaves, and the fruit is from its beginning to its end, so it has no visible trunk." Masruq said: "The trees of Paradise are layered from their bottoms to their tops."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and shade extended﴾, i.e., perpetual, not abolished by the sun.

﴿and water poured out﴾, i.e., flowing, not cut off.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿neither cut off nor forbidden﴾. Concerning it there are three opinions.

The first: not cut off at one time and not at another, nor forbidden by walls and guards; rather it is available to whoever wants it. This is the saying of Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid and Qatadah. Some summarized it by saying: "Not cut off by times, nor forbidden by prices."

The second: it is not cut off when it is picked, nor is it prevented from anyone who desires it. This was related from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The third: it is not cut off by perishing, nor forbidden by decay. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and raised couches﴾. Concerning it there are two opinions.

One: they are the cushions spread for sitting and sleeping. Concerning their being raised there are two opinions: one is that they are raised above the thrones; the second is that their being raised means the increase of their stuffing so that enjoyment of them may be pleasant.

The second: the intended meaning of "bed" (firash) is women; the Arabs call a woman "firash," "izar," and "libas." Concerning the meaning of their being raised there are three opinions: one is that they are raised in beauty above the women of the people of this world; the second is that they are raised above impurities; the third is that they are raised in the hearts due to the intensity of inclination towards them.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We have produced them with a [special] production﴾, meaning the women. Ibn Qutaybah said: "He sufficed with mentioning the beds, since they are the place of the women, instead of mentioning them." Concerning those referred to there are two opinions.

One: they are the believing women of the people of this world. Then concerning their production there are two opinions: one is that their production is their resurrection from the graves, said by Ibn ʿAbbas; the second is their restoration after old age and decrepitude as virgins, young, said by al-Dahhak.

The second: they are the wide-eyed maidens (al-hur al-ʿin), and their production is their creation without birth, said by al-Zajjaj. The correct view is that it is said: the production includes all of them; the maidens were produced originally, and the believing women were produced by restoration and change of attributes. Anas ibn Malik related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "Among those produced who were in this world are old women, blear-eyed and rheumy-eyed."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and We made them virgins﴾, i.e., maidens. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "Her husband does not come to her except that he finds her a virgin."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿loving, of equal age﴾. Al-Jumhur recited ʿuruban with a damma on the ra'. Hamzah and Khalaf recited it with a sukun on the ra'. Ibn Jarir said: "It is the dialect of Tamim and Bakr."

Regarding the meaning of "ʿuruban" the exegetes have five opinions.

One: they are those who are lovingly devoted to their husbands. This was narrated by al-ʿAwfi from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Saʿid ibn Jubayr, Ibn Qutaybah and al-Zajjaj also said so.

The second: they are passionately loving (al-ʿawashiq). This was narrated by ʿAli ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn ʿAbbas, and al-Hasan, Qatadah, Muqatil and al-Mubarrad also said so; and from Mujahid, as in the two sayings.

The third: those good in their conjugal relations (al-hasanah al-tabbuʿul). This was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Abu ʿUbaydah said so.

The fourth: the coquettish (al-ghanijat). This was said by ʿIkrimah.

The fifth: those good in speech. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

As for "al-atrab" (equal in age), we have mentioned them in [p. 52].

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿A multitude from the earlier peoples﴾ ﴿and a multitude from the later peoples﴾. This is part of the description of the companions of the right hand. Concerning "the earlier" and "the later" there is disagreement, and its explanation has already preceded [al-Waqi'ah: 13]. Muqatil claimed that when the first verse was revealed, which is His saying: ﴿and few from the later peoples﴾, the believers felt great grief over it until ﴿and a multitude from the later peoples﴾ was revealed, and it abrogated it. A similar meaning was related from ʿUrwah ibn Ruwaym.

I say: the claim of abrogation here has no basis, for three reasons.

One: the scholars of abrogation and abrogated texts did not agree on this.

The second: the discourse in both verses is informational, and information is not subject to abrogation; [so there is no basis for it here].

The third: "thullah" means a group and a band; al-Zajjaj said: "Their derivation is from a piece, and 'thall' means breaking and cutting." Based on this, it is possible that "thullah" carries the meaning of "few."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Among lote trees with thorns removed﴾. The occasion of its revelation: the Muslims looked at Wajj, which is a valley in al-Ta'if, fertile, and its lote trees (sidr) impressed them, so they said: "Would that we had the like of this!" Then this verse was revealed. This was related by Abu al-ʿAliyah and al-Dahhak.

Regarding al-makhdud (with thorns removed) there are three opinions.

The first: it is the one that has no thorns. This was narrated by Abu Talhah from Ibn ʿAbbas, and ʿIkrimah and Qusamah ibn Zuhayr also said so. Ibn Qutaybah said: "It is as if its thorns were cut off (khudida), i.e., uprooted." From this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ about Madinah: "Its thorns shall not be cut off."

The second: it is the one laden with fruit. This was narrated by al-ʿAwfi from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Mujahid and al-Dahhak also said so.

The third: it is the one laden with fruit that has no thorns. This was mentioned by Qatadah.

Regarding al-talh (acacia) there are two opinions.

One: it is the banana tree (al-mawz). This was said by ʿAli, Ibn ʿAbbas, Abu Hurayrah, Abu Saʿid al-Khudri, [al-Hasan], ʿAta', ʿIkrimah, Mujahid and Qatadah.

The second: it is large trees with big thorns. Abu ʿUbaydah said: "This is the talh among the Arabs." The camel driver (al-Hadi) said:

*Her guide gave her good news and said: "Tomorrow you will see the acacia and the mountains."*

If it is asked: what is the benefit of the talh?

The answer: it has blossoms and a pleasant fragrance, so He promised them what they know and incline towards, even though there is no equality between it and what is in this world. Mujahid said: "They used to admire Wajj, its shade, its acacias and its lote trees." As for al-mandud (layered, arranged), Ibn Qutaybah said: "It is the one that is arranged with fruit or leaves, and the fruit is from its beginning to its end, so it has no visible trunk." Masruq said: "The trees of Paradise are layered from their bottoms to their tops."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and shade extended﴾, i.e., perpetual, not abolished by the sun.

﴿and water poured out﴾, i.e., flowing, not cut off.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿neither cut off nor forbidden﴾. Concerning it there are three opinions.

The first: not cut off at one time and not at another, nor forbidden by walls and guards; rather it is available to whoever wants it. This is the saying of Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid and Qatadah. Some summarized it by saying: "Not cut off by times, nor forbidden by prices."

The second: it is not cut off when it is picked, nor is it prevented from anyone who desires it. This was related from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The third: it is not cut off by perishing, nor forbidden by decay. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and raised couches﴾. Concerning it there are two opinions.

One: they are the cushions spread for sitting and sleeping. Concerning their being raised there are two opinions: one is that they are raised above the thrones; the second is that their being raised means the increase of their stuffing so that enjoyment of them may be pleasant.

The second: the intended meaning of "bed" (firash) is women; the Arabs call a woman "firash," "izar," and "libas." Concerning the meaning of their being raised there are three opinions: one is that they are raised in beauty above the women of the people of this world; the second is that they are raised above impurities; the third is that they are raised in the hearts due to the intensity of inclination towards them.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We have produced them with a [special] production﴾, meaning the women. Ibn Qutaybah said: "He sufficed with mentioning the beds, since they are the place of the women, instead of mentioning them." Concerning those referred to there are two opinions.

One: they are the believing women of the people of this world. Then concerning their production there are two opinions: one is that their production is their resurrection from the graves, said by Ibn ʿAbbas; the second is their restoration after old age and decrepitude as virgins, young, said by al-Dahhak.

The second: they are the wide-eyed maidens (al-hur al-ʿin), and their production is their creation without birth, said by al-Zajjaj. The correct view is that it is said: the production includes all of them; the maidens were produced originally, and the believing women were produced by restoration and change of attributes. Anas ibn Malik related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "Among those produced who were in this world are old women, blear-eyed and rheumy-eyed."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and We made them virgins﴾, i.e., maidens. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "Her husband does not come to her except that he finds her a virgin."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿loving, of equal age﴾. Al-Jumhur recited ʿuruban with a damma on the ra'. Hamzah and Khalaf recited it with a sukun on the ra'. Ibn Jarir said: "It is the dialect of Tamim and Bakr."

Regarding the meaning of "ʿuruban" the exegetes have five opinions.

One: they are those who are lovingly devoted to their husbands. This was narrated by al-ʿAwfi from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Saʿid ibn Jubayr, Ibn Qutaybah and al-Zajjaj also said so.

The second: they are passionately loving (al-ʿawashiq). This was narrated by ʿAli ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn ʿAbbas, and al-Hasan, Qatadah, Muqatil and al-Mubarrad also said so; and from Mujahid, as in the two sayings.

The third: those good in their conjugal relations (al-hasanah al-tabbuʿul). This was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Abu ʿUbaydah said so.

The fourth: the coquettish (al-ghanijat). This was said by ʿIkrimah.

The fifth: those good in speech. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

As for "al-atrab" (equal in age), we have mentioned them in [p. 52].

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿A multitude from the earlier peoples﴾ ﴿and a multitude from the later peoples﴾. This is part of the description of the companions of the right hand. Concerning "the earlier" and "the later" there is disagreement, and its explanation has already preceded [al-Waqi'ah: 13]. Muqatil claimed that when the first verse was revealed, which is His saying: ﴿and few from the later peoples﴾, the believers felt great grief over it until ﴿and a multitude from the later peoples﴾ was revealed, and it abrogated it. A similar meaning was related from ʿUrwah ibn Ruwaym.

I say: the claim of abrogation here has no basis, for three reasons.

One: the scholars of abrogation and abrogated texts did not agree on this.

The second: the discourse in both verses is informational, and information is not subject to abrogation; [so there is no basis for it here].

The third: "thullah" means a group and a band; al-Zajjaj said: "Their derivation is from a piece, and 'thall' means breaking and cutting." Based on this, it is possible that "thullah" carries the meaning of "few."

**(p-144)** His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿What are the companions of the left?﴾ We have already explained that this is in the sense of wonder at their condition. The meaning is: what is their state, and what evil has been prepared for them? Then He explained to them the evil of their final return, saying: ﴿In scorching wind and boiling water﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: it is the heat of the Fire.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And a shade of black smoke﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: a shade of smoke. Al-Farra' said: al-yahmum is black smoke. ﴿Neither cool nor pleasant﴾. The grammatically proper reading is the genitive (khafd), following what precedes it, and similar to it is ﴿an olive tree, neither of the east nor of the west﴾ [al-Nur: 35]. Likewise His saying: ﴿And fruit abundant﴾ ﴿neither cut off nor forbidden﴾. If you put the nominative after "la" it would also be correct. The Arabs make the word "karim" (pleasant) follow whatever they negate with a verb intended as blame. They say: "This house is not spacious nor pleasant," and "This is not fat nor pleasant."

Ibn 'Abbas said: neither cold in its entrance nor pleasant in its appearance.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, they were before that﴾, that is, in the world, ﴿affluent﴾, that is, living in luxury in abandoning the command of Allah, so their affluence occupied them from reflection and worship.

﴿And they used to persist﴾, that is, to remain ﴿in the great sin﴾. Regarding this there are four views.

The first: it is shirk (associating partners with Allah). This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd.

The second: it is the great sin from which they do not repent. This was said by Mujahid, and it is related from Qatadah as in the two views (above).

The third: it is the perjurious oath (al-yamin al-ghamus). This was said by al-Sha'bi.

The fourth: it is shirk and disbelief in the Resurrection. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And our forefathers, the earlier ones?﴾ Abu 'Ubaydah said: the waw is vowelled because it is not the waw of "or" (aw), but rather "wa-abaana," and the interrogative alif entered upon it, so it was left with a fatha. The people of Medina and Ibn 'Amir read "aw abaa'unaa" with the waw sukun.

**(p-145)** The explanation of what was not mentioned here has preceded [Hud: 103; al-Saffat: 62; al-An'am: 70], up to His saying: ﴿So you will drink as drinking thirsty camels﴾. The people of Medina, 'Asim and Hamzah read "shurb" with a damma on the shin; the rest read it with a fatha. Al-Farra' said: the Arabs say "shiribtuhu shurban," but most of the people of Najd say "sharban" with a fatha. My teachers recited to me:

"A morsel of a slice from the roast suffices him if he comes upon it, and a single gulp from the ghumar suffices his drink."

Al-Kisa'i claimed that a group from the Banu Sa'd ibn Tamim say "shirb al-Him" with a kasra. Al-Zajjaj said: "al-sharb" is the verbal noun, and "al-shurb" with a damma is the noun. He said: it has also been said that it is a verbal noun too.

Regarding "al-Him" there are two views.

The first: the thirsty camels. This was related by Ibn Abi Talhah and al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas, and Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, 'Ata', al-Dahhak and Qatadah said the same. Ibn Qutaybah said: they are camels that are afflicted with a disease so that they do not quench their thirst with water. It is said: a camel that is "ahyam," and a female camel that is "hayma'."

The second: it is the sandy land that does not quench its thirst with water. This is also related from Ibn 'Abbas. Abu 'Ubaydah said: al-Him is what does not become sated of sand or of camels.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿This is their nuzul (hospitality)﴾, that is, their provision. 'Abbas related from Abu 'Amr that it is read "nuzlu-hum" with the zay sukun, that is, their provision and their food. Regarding "al-Din" there are two views, which we have mentioned in al-Fatihah.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 56, verses 57–62:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿We created you﴾, meaning: We brought you into existence when you were nothing, and you acknowledge this. "Then why do you not" meaning: why will you not "believe" in the Resurrection?

Then he argued for their resurrection by the power to originate them, saying: ﴿Have you considered that which you emit?﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: meaning, that which comes from you of semen (al-maniyy). It is said: amnā al-rajul yumnī and manā yamnī. Accordingly, "tumnūn" with an opening fatha on the ta' is permissible, if a transmission supports it.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Is it you who create it, or are We the Creator?﴾ Meaning: do you create what you emit as a human being? In this there is an alert to two things.

The first: a reminder of favour, since He created a complete human from the despised water.

The second: whoever is able to create what you have witnessed of the origin of your existence is more able to create what is hidden from you, which is your re-creation.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿We have decreed death among you﴾. Ibn Kathir read "qaddarnā" with a light dal. There are two views regarding the meaning of the statement.

The first: We have decreed death upon you.

The second: We have made you equal in death. "And We are not to be outdone, in replacing your likes" Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: if We wish to create a creation other than you, no one will precede Us (p-147) in it, and that will not escape Us. Ibn Qutayba said: We are not overpowered in substituting others like you in your place.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We will make you into what you do not know﴾. On this there are four views.

The first: We change your attributes and make you apes and swine, as We did with those before you. This is the view of al-Hasan.

The second: We will bring you into being in the crops of black birds that are in Barhut, as if they were swallows. This is the view of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab.

The third: We create you in whatever form We wish. This is the view of Mujahid.

The fourth: We create you in other than your form. This is the view of al-Suddi. Muqatil said: We create you other than your creation, in forms you do not know.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And you have already known the first creation﴾, which is the initial origination when He created you from a drop (nutfa) and a clinging clot (ʿalaqa). ﴿Then why do you not remember?﴾ meaning: why will you not take heed, so that you know the power of Allah and thereby acknowledge the Resurrection?

**Ibn al-Jawzi, *Zad al-Masir*, on Surat al-Waqi'a (56:75–82)**

The first view is that the *fa* (فَ) is emphatic (*tawkid*), and the meaning is "so I swear." A parallel is ﴿so that the People of the Book may know﴾ (59:29). Al-Zajjaj said this is the view of Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The second view is that the *fa* retains its original meaning, and there are two explanations of what it means.

The first is that it refers back to what came before, and its meaning is a prohibition. The sense of the sentence is: "Do not lie, and do not deny the blessings and proofs I have mentioned." This was said by al-Mawardi.

The second is that *la* (لا) is a rejection of what the disbelievers say about the Qur'an: that it is magic, poetry, or soothsaying. Then an oath is begun to affirm that it is a noble Qur'an. This was said by Ali ibn Ahmad al-Naysaburi. Al-Hasan recited *"fa-la-uqsimu"* (فَلَأُقْسِمُ) without an *alif* between the *lam* and the *hamza*.

Allah's words, ﴿*bi-mawaqi'*﴾ (بِمَواقِعِ, "by the places of fall"), are read by Hamza and al-Kisa'i as *bi-mawqi'* (بِمَوْقِعِ) in the singular. Abu Ali (al-Farisi) said that *mawaqi'* means *masaqit* (places where they fall). Whoever reads it in the singular does so because it is a collective noun (*ism jins*). Whoever reads it in the plural does so because the places differ.

There are two views about "the stars" (*al-nujum*).

The first is that they are the stars of the sky. This was said by most scholars. On this view, there are three explanations of *mawaqi'ha* (their places of fall):
- Their scattering and dispersal on the Day of Resurrection. This was said by al-Hasan.
- Their stations (*manazil*). This was said by Ata and Qatada.
- Their setting in the west. This was said by Abu Ubayda.

The second is that they are the stars of the Qur'an, related by Ibn Jubayr from Ibn Abbas. On this view, they are called "stars" because they were revealed in separate parts (*mutafarriqa*), and their *mawaqi'* is their revelation.

Allah's words, ﴿*wa-innahu la-qasam*﴾ (وَإنَّهُ لَقَسَمٌ, "and indeed it is an oath"), the pronoun *ha'* (هاء) refers to the oath.

There is inversion (*taqdim wa-ta'khir*) in the sentence. Its intended meaning is: "And indeed it is a mighty oath, if only you knew its greatness." Then the thing sworn to is mentioned: ﴿indeed it is a noble Qur'an﴾. *Karim* (noble) is a comprehensive term for what is praised. The Qur'an contains clarification, guidance, and wisdom, and it is honoured by Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

Allah's words, ﴿*fi kitab*﴾ (فِي كِتابٍ, "in a Book"), have two views.

The first is that it is the Preserved Tablet (*al-Lawh al-Mahfuz*). This was said by Ibn Abbas. The second is that it is the *mushaf* (the codex) in our hands. This was said by Mujahid and Qatada.

The word *"maknun"* (مَكْنُونِ, "hidden" or "guarded") has two views.

The first is that it is hidden from creation. This was said by Muqatil, and this is according to the first view (that the Book is the Preserved Tablet).

The second is that it is protected. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

Allah's words, ﴿*la yamassuhu illa al-mutahharun*﴾ (لا يَمَسُّهُ إلا المُطَهَّرُونَ, "none touches it except the purified"), are as follows. Whoever says that the Book is the Preserved Tablet takes *al-mutahharun* (المُطَهَّرُونَ) to mean the angels. This is the view of Ibn Abbas, Ikrima, Mujahid, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr. On this view, the sentence is a statement of fact (*khabar*).

Whoever says that the Book is the *mushaf* has four views about *al-mutahharun*:
- They are those purified from ritual impurities (*ahdath*). This was said by the majority. On this view, the apparent sense is a negation, but its meaning is a prohibition.
- They are those purified from *shirk* (polytheism). This was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib.
- They are those purified from sins and faults. This was said by al-Rabi' ibn Anas.
- The meaning of the sentence is that none finds its taste and benefit except those who believe in it. This was related by al-Farra'.

Allah's word, ﴿*tanzil*﴾ (تَنْزِيلٌ, "a revelation"), means: it is a revelation (*tanzil*). The meaning is: it is something sent down (*munazzal*). The thing sent down is called *tanzil* by a broad use of the language, just as one says of what is decreed, "*qadar*" (decree), and of what is created, "*khalq*" (creation).

Allah's words, ﴿*afa-bihadha al-hadith*﴾ (أفَبِهَذا الحَدِيثِ, "Is it then this discourse"), mean the Qur'an. ﴿*Antum mudhinun*﴾ (أنْتُمْ مُدْهِنُونَ, "are you compromisers?") has two views.

The first is "deniers" (*mukadhdhibun*). This was said by Ibn Abbas, al-Dahhak, and al-Farra'.

The second is those who collude with the disbelievers in disbelief in it. This was said by Mujahid. Abu Ubayda said *al-mudhin* (المَدْهِنُ) means *al-mudahin* (one who compromises). Ibn Qutayba likewise said *mudhinun* means *mudahinun*. It is said: "He compromised in his religion" (*adhhana fi dinihi*) and "he compromised" (*dahana*).

Allah's words, ﴿*wa-taj'alna rizqakum annakum tukadhdhibun*﴾ (وَتَجْعَلُونَ رِزْقَكم أنَّكم تُكَذِّبُونَ, "and you make your provision the denial"), Muslim related in his *Sahih*, from the *hadith* (a report of the Prophet's words and actions) of Ibn Abbas, who said: "The people were given rain in the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and the Prophet ﷺ said: 'In the morning, some of the people are thankful, and some of them are disbelievers.' They said: 'This is a mercy that Allah placed where He willed.' Some of them said: 'The *nawʾ* (the rising or setting of a star, a folk belief for rain) of such-and-such has indeed come true,' and then this verse was revealed: ﴿So I swear by the places of the stars﴾ until His words ﴿that you deny﴾."

The first view is that the *fa* (فَ) is emphatic (*tawkid*), and the meaning is "so I swear." A parallel is ﴿so that the People of the Book may know﴾ (59:29). Al-Zajjaj said this is the view of Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The second view is that the *fa* retains its original meaning, and there are two explanations of what it means.

The first is that it refers back to what came before, and its meaning is a prohibition. The sense of the sentence is: "Do not lie, and do not deny the blessings and proofs I have mentioned." This was said by al-Mawardi.

The second is that *la* (لا) is a rejection of what the disbelievers say about the Qur'an: that it is magic, poetry, or soothsaying. Then an oath is begun to affirm that it is a noble Qur'an. This was said by Ali ibn Ahmad al-Naysaburi. Al-Hasan recited *"fa-la-uqsimu"* (فَلَأُقْسِمُ) without an *alif* between the *lam* and the *hamza*.

Allah's words, ﴿*bi-mawaqi'*﴾ (بِمَواقِعِ, "by the places of fall"), are read by Hamza and al-Kisa'i as *bi-mawqi'* (بِمَوْقِعِ) in the singular. Abu Ali (al-Farisi) said that *mawaqi'* means *masaqit* (places where they fall). Whoever reads it in the singular does so because it is a collective noun (*ism jins*). Whoever reads it in the plural does so because the places differ.

There are two views about "the stars" (*al-nujum*).

The first is that they are the stars of the sky. This was said by most scholars. On this view, there are three explanations of *mawaqi'ha* (their places of fall):
- Their scattering and dispersal on the Day of Resurrection. This was said by al-Hasan.
- Their stations (*manazil*). This was said by Ata and Qatada.
- Their setting in the west. This was said by Abu Ubayda.

The second is that they are the stars of the Qur'an, related by Ibn Jubayr from Ibn Abbas. On this view, they are called "stars" because they were revealed in separate parts (*mutafarriqa*), and their *mawaqi'* is their revelation.

Allah's words, ﴿*wa-innahu la-qasam*﴾ (وَإنَّهُ لَقَسَمٌ, "and indeed it is an oath"), the pronoun *ha'* (هاء) refers to the oath.

There is inversion (*taqdim wa-ta'khir*) in the sentence. Its intended meaning is: "And indeed it is a mighty oath, if only you knew its greatness." Then the thing sworn to is mentioned: ﴿indeed it is a noble Qur'an﴾. *Karim* (noble) is a comprehensive term for what is praised. The Qur'an contains clarification, guidance, and wisdom, and it is honoured by Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

Allah's words, ﴿*fi kitab*﴾ (فِي كِتابٍ, "in a Book"), have two views.

The first is that it is the Preserved Tablet (*al-Lawh al-Mahfuz*). This was said by Ibn Abbas. The second is that it is the *mushaf* (the codex) in our hands. This was said by Mujahid and Qatada.

The word *"maknun"* (مَكْنُونِ, "hidden" or "guarded") has two views.

The first is that it is hidden from creation. This was said by Muqatil, and this is according to the first view (that the Book is the Preserved Tablet).

The second is that it is protected. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

Allah's words, ﴿*la yamassuhu illa al-mutahharun*﴾ (لا يَمَسُّهُ إلا المُطَهَّرُونَ, "none touches it except the purified"), are as follows. Whoever says that the Book is the Preserved Tablet takes *al-mutahharun* (المُطَهَّرُونَ) to mean the angels. This is the view of Ibn Abbas, Ikrima, Mujahid, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr. On this view, the sentence is a statement of fact (*khabar*).

Whoever says that the Book is the *mushaf* has four views about *al-mutahharun*:
- They are those purified from ritual impurities (*ahdath*). This was said by the majority. On this view, the apparent sense is a negation, but its meaning is a prohibition.
- They are those purified from *shirk* (polytheism). This was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib.
- They are those purified from sins and faults. This was said by al-Rabi' ibn Anas.
- The meaning of the sentence is that none finds its taste and benefit except those who believe in it. This was related by al-Farra'.

Allah's word, ﴿*tanzil*﴾ (تَنْزِيلٌ, "a revelation"), means: it is a revelation (*tanzil*). The meaning is: it is something sent down (*munazzal*). The thing sent down is called *tanzil* by a broad use of the language, just as one says of what is decreed, "*qadar*" (decree), and of what is created, "*khalq*" (creation).

Allah's words, ﴿*afa-bihadha al-hadith*﴾ (أفَبِهَذا الحَدِيثِ, "Is it then this discourse"), mean the Qur'an. ﴿*Antum mudhinun*﴾ (أنْتُمْ مُدْهِنُونَ, "are you compromisers?") has two views.

The first is "deniers" (*mukadhdhibun*). This was said by Ibn Abbas, al-Dahhak, and al-Farra'.

The second is those who collude with the disbelievers in disbelief in it. This was said by Mujahid. Abu Ubayda said *al-mudhin* (المَدْهِنُ) means *al-mudahin* (one who compromises). Ibn Qutayba likewise said *mudhinun* means *mudahinun*. It is said: "He compromised in his religion" (*adhhana fi dinihi*) and "he compromised" (*dahana*).

Allah's words, ﴿*wa-taj'alna rizqakum annakum tukadhdhibun*﴾ (وَتَجْعَلُونَ رِزْقَكم أنَّكم تُكَذِّبُونَ, "and you make your provision the denial"), Muslim related in his *Sahih*, from the *hadith* (a report of the Prophet's words and actions) of Ibn Abbas, who said: "The people were given rain in the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and the Prophet ﷺ said: 'In the morning, some of the people are thankful, and some of them are disbelievers.' They said: 'This is a mercy that Allah placed where He willed.' Some of them said: 'The *nawʾ* (the rising or setting of a star, a folk belief for rain) of such-and-such has indeed come true,' and then this verse was revealed: ﴿So I swear by the places of the stars﴾ until His words ﴿that you deny﴾."

Al-Bukhari and Muslim related in the two *Sahihs*, from the *hadith* of Zayd ibn Khalid al-Juhani, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ led us in a prayer at al-Hudaybiyya, after a rain that had fallen during the night. When he finished, he turned to the people and said: 'Do you know what your Lord said?' They said: 'Allah and His Messenger know best.' He said: 'He said: In the morning, some of My servants are believers in Me, and some are disbelievers. As for the one who believes, he says: We have been given rain by the grace and mercy of Allah; that is a believer in Me and a disbeliever in the stars. As for the one who says: We have been given rain by the *nawʾ* of such-and-such, that is a disbeliever in Me and a believer in the stars.'"

The commentators have three views about the meaning of this verse.

The first is that *rizq* (provision) here means *shukr* (thanks). ʿA'isha related from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that he said, concerning ﴿and you make your provision﴾: "Your thanks." This is the view of Ali ibn Abi Talib and Ibn Abbas. Ali used to recite *"wa-taj'alna shukrakum"* (وَتَجْعَلُونَ شُكْرَكُمْ, "and you make your thanks").

The second is that the meaning is: "and you make the thanks for your provision to be your denial." This was said by most scholars. This is because they used to be given rain, and they would say: "We were given rain by the *nawʾ* of such-and-such."

The third is that *rizq* means *hazz* (portion). The meaning is: "and you make your portion and share of the Qur'an to be that you deny it." This was mentioned by al-Tha'labi. Ubayy ibn Ka'b and al-Mufaddal, from Asim, read *"tukadhdhibun"* (تَكْذِبُونَ) with an open *ta'* (تَ), a sukun on the *kaf* (كْ), and a light *dhal* (ذِ).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 56, verse 83–96:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then why not﴾, i.e., "why then not" (fahalla), ﴿when it reaches the throat (ḥulqūm)﴾, meaning: the soul (nafs). Its mention is omitted because the context indicates it. They recited as evidence of this:

؎ When it rattles (in the throat) one day, and the chest is constricted by it

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and you﴾, meaning the people of the dying person, ﴿are looking on﴾ at the authority and command of Allah. A second view: you are looking at the human being in that state, and you possess nothing to help him. ﴿And We are nearer to him than you are﴾. Regarding this there are two views:

The first: the Angel of Death is nearer to him than his family, ﴿but you do not see﴾ the angels. This was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas.

The second: We are nearer to him than you by knowledge, power and sight, ﴿but you do not see﴾, i.e., you do not know. The address is to the disbelievers. This was mentioned by al-Wahidi.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿not being repaid (ghayra madinīn)﴾. Regarding this there are five views.

The first: "not being called to account" (muḥāsabīn). This was narrated by al-Dahhak from Ibn Abbas, and al-Hasan, Ibn Jubayr, ʿAtaʾ and ʿIkrima said the same. The second: "certain" (mūqinīn), said by Mujahid. The third: "resurrected" (mabʿūthīn), said by Qatada. The fourth: "recompensed" (majziyyīn). From this one says: "dintuhu" (I repaid him), and "as you do, so it will be done to you" (kamā tadīnu tudān), said by Abu ʿUbayda. The fifth: "subjugated, humbled" (mamlūkīn adhillāʾ), from your saying: "dint lahu bil-ṭāʿa" (I submitted to him in obedience), said by Ibn Qutayba.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿you return it﴾, i.e., you return the soul. The meaning: if you deny the God who calls you to account and recompenses you, then why do you not return this soul? If you are unable to do that, then know that the matter belongs to others than you.

Al-Farrāʾ said: His saying, ﴿you return it﴾, is the answer to His saying, ﴿Then why not, when it reaches the throat﴾, and to His saying, ﴿Then why not, if you are not being repaid﴾; for both are answered by a single answer. A similar case is His saying: ﴿So whoever follows My guidance, no fear shall be upon them﴾ [al-Baqara: 38]. Then He mentioned the classes of creation at death, and said, exalted is He: ﴿But if he is of those brought near﴾, meaning: the one whose soul has reached the throat is among "those brought near" (al-muqarrabīn) to Allah. Abu al-ʿĀliya said: they are the foremost (al-sābiqūn). ﴿Then there is rest (rawḥ)﴾, i.e., for him there is rest. The majority pronounce the rāʾ with a fatḥa. Regarding its meaning there are six views.

The first: joy (al-faraḥ), narrated by Saʿid ibn Jubayr from Ibn Abbas. The second: ease (al-rāḥa), narrated by Abu Talha from Ibn Abbas. The third: forgiveness and mercy, narrated by al-ʿAwfi from Ibn Abbas. The fourth: Paradise, said by Mujahid. The fifth: relief from the distress they were in, said by Muhammad ibn Kaʿb. The sixth: rest in the grave, i.e., pleasant breeze, said by Ibn Qutayba. Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, Abu Razin, al-Hasan, ʿIkrima, Ibn Yaʿmar, Qatada, Ruways from Yaʿqub, and Ibn Abi Surayj from al-Kisāʾī recited: "fa-rūḥun" with a ḍamma on the rāʾ. Regarding the meaning of this reading there are two views.

The first: that its meaning is "then mercy," said by Qatada.

The second: "then life and continuance," said by Ibn Qutayba. al-Zajjāj said: its meaning is: then everlasting life in which there is no death. Regarding "al-rayḥān" (sweet basil/provision) there are four views.

The first: that it is provision (al-rizq), narrated by Saʿid ibn Jubayr from Ibn Abbas.

The second: that it is repose (al-mustarāḥ), narrated by Ibn Abi Talha from Ibn Abbas.

The third: that it is Paradise, said by Mujahid and Qatada.

The fourth: that it is fragrant basil. Abu al-ʿĀliya said: none of those brought near from among the worldly will depart until he is brought a branch of the basil of Paradise, and he smells it, and then his soul is taken within it. Al-Hasan went in this direction too. Abu ʿImran al-Jawni said: we have been told that when the soul of the believer is taken, bundles of basil from Paradise are cast upon him, and his soul is placed within them.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then peace be upon you from the companions of the right (aṣḥāb al-yamīn)﴾. Regarding this there are three views.

The first: "Then safety is yours from the punishment," said by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas.

The second: the angels greet him and inform him that he is of the companions of the right, said by ʿAtaʾ.

The third: the meaning is that you see among them what you love of safety, and you know what has been prepared for them of recompense, said by al-Zajjaj.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But if he is of the deniers﴾, i.e., of those who deny the resurrection, the ﴿misguided (al-ḍāllīn)﴾ from guidance, ﴿then (there is) a welcome (nuzul)﴾. We have explained this in this surah [al-Waqiʿa: 56].

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, this is the truth of certainty (ḥaqq al-yaqīn)﴾, meaning: what has been mentioned in this surah. I.e., it is certainty in truth; he attributed it to itself, as in your saying "ṣalāt al-ūlā" and "ṣalāt al-ʿaṣr," and similar to it: ﴿And the abode of the Hereafter﴾ [Yusuf: 109]. This meaning has already preceded. Some said: its meaning is: and indeed it is truly for the God-fearing. It has also been said that "certainty" is applied to the truth.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So glorify the name of your Lord﴾. We have mentioned this in this surah [al-Waqiʿa: 74].
